doc.title: Håkan Rydin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016

title: 'Here, There and Everywhere' and 'Where Have All the Flowers Gone' at the Glasgow concert
summary: Rowe praises the previous night's trio set; Rydin explains the Beatles ballad and the Pete Seeger song, including a Hanoi listener moved to tears.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It’s your agent with your next gig.
Yeah right. No but I think you mentioned, I was going to talk about this later, but I had the pleasure of hearing your trio yesterday.
And I thought you mentioned something about The Beatles.
And then you played “Here, There and Everywhere” and boy it got me.
Because we had just come from Liverpool and did the whole Beatles — like a pilgrimage. And when you played that song I thought it was wonderful.
Thank you. You recognized it. I played definitely in jazz style, not in pop style. As a jazz ballad.
Yes. Well I could tell you have, in my opinion, you have great respect for the melody.

And you went from that, I was taking notes, and you picked the tempo up and then you were playing this other song and I’m going what is that song. And was I wrong or was it “Where Have All the Flowers Gone”?
You are so correct. Yes. I think I forgot to mention it. But I said I’ve got to play something which I heard when I grew up. Yeah. It’s from Pete Seeger. I think I never heard it in jazz circles.

In fact I’ve played this song, I’ve played it for a couple of years, not too very long, but I played it in Hanoi, an American guy, in fact I think it was a couple, but a guy came up to me afterwards and he was crying. Because he had such strong memories of the song. So he was touched and me too. It was so nice.
Yeah. It’s sort of iconic in the States because the Kingston Trio did it after Pete Seeger, and sometimes people play it in church.
Yes. And it’s been translated into many languages.
